title: Ireland's election to the United Nations Human Rights Council for the 2027-2029 term: opportunities and challenges
dek: Ireland will take up an important UN role in 2027, with a chance to promote and protect human rights.
abstract: As a Member State of the United Nations (UN) Human Rights Council (2027-2029), Ireland can harness its vote and diplomatic resources to promote and protect human rights at a critical time, as the world experiences rising rates of armed conflict and declining economic support for the UN’s human rights pillar.

content.text: , which created the UNHRC, candidate States must receive the support of a majority of UNGA Member States voting in a secret ballot in order to be appointed (currently 97 votes). There are no mandatory membership criteria concerning human rights performance. However, when voting UNGA Member States must take into account any voluntary pledges and commitments made by candidate States, as well as their contribution to the promotion and protection of human rights. States are ineligible for immediate re-election after serving two consecutive UNHRC membership terms.
Ireland belongs to the Western European and Others regional group (WEOG), which has seven UNHRC membership seats. On

requires UNHRC Member States to uphold the highest standards in promoting and protecting human rights. UNGA, by a two-thirds majority of its Members present and voting, can resolve to suspend a UNHRC Member State that commits gross and systematic human rights violations. However, to date, this power has only been used on two occasions, when UNGA resolved to suspend Libya in 2011 and Russia in 2022.

Non-UNHRC Member States can participate in the UNHRC’s work as observer States. Whilst observer States lack voting rights, they can participate in negotiations concerning, and co-sponsor, draft UNHRC resolutions. They can also make oral interventions during the Council’s general debates, panel discussions and interactive dialogues.

In situations where States receive similar human rights-related recommendations from multiple sources, it can be difficult to determine which, if any, was the main trigger for a decision to implement the substance of the recommendation. The sheer volume of recommendations received from various international, regional and domestic human rights mechanisms can pose an implementation challenge for States. As a UNHRC Member State, Ireland can harness not only its vote, but also its diplomatic resources, to help build the cross-regional backing necessary for initiatives it supports. Ireland can also count toward the quorum necessary to convene special sessions. Furthermore, Ireland can champion its five membership priorities, fulfil its candidature
to defend the independence of special procedures, and make contributions during interactive dialogues, general debates, panel discussions and UPR reviews.
